ClientConnect is a keyboard-driven desktop address book for insurance agents who manage large client portfolios. This
guide explains how ClientConnect is designed and implemented, for developers who want to maintain or extend it. To
learn how to use the app, see the [User Guide](UserGuide.html).

* ClientConnect is based on [AddressBook-Level3](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3) (AB3) by the [SE-EDU initiative](https://se-education.org). * Third-party libraries used: [JavaFX](https://openjfx.io/) for the GUI, [Jackson](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson) for reading and writing JSON data files, and [JUnit 5](https://junit.org/junit5/) for testing.

The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W08-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W08-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
**How the architecture components interact with each other**

Each of the four main components (also shown in the diagram above),

* provides its functionality through a concrete `{Component Name}Manager` class that implements the corresponding API interface.

This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.
The `find` command filters the displayed client list by name keywords and/or tags. The following sequence diagram shows a successful search using `find Alice t/friends`.
![Sequence diagram for finding clients by name or tag](images/FindSequenceDiagram.png)
1. `LogicManager` passes the command text to `AddressBookParser`, which delegates the arguments to `FindCommandParser`.

2. `FindCommandParser` trims and normalizes whitespace, then uses `ArgumentTokenizer` to separate name keywords in the preamble from `t/` tag values. It validates each tag using `ParserUtil.parseTag()`.

3. The parser creates a `NameContainsKeywordsPredicate` for a name-only search, or a `NameOrTagContainsKeywordsPredicate` when tags are supplied, and passes that predicate to a new `FindCommand`. Tag-only searches use the latter predicate with an empty name-keyword list.

4. `FindCommand.execute(model)` calls `Model.updateFilteredPersonList(predicate)`. `ModelManager` sets the predicate on its internal `FilteredList`, applying the search to the full client list. Names match any keyword as a case-insensitive substring; tags match any complete tag value, also ignoring case. These conditions are combined with **OR**, so the example matches clients whose names contain `Alice` or whose tags include `friends`.

5. The command reads the size of `Model.getFilteredPersonList()` and returns a `CommandResult` containing the number of matches, including zero when no clients match. The UI observes the filtered and sorted list and displays the matching clients.

Empty arguments or invalid tags cause a `ParseException` during parsing, before a `FindCommand` is created or the displayed list is changed. Finding clients changes the list filter without modifying client records. The diagram focuses on parsing and filtering; the usual `LogicManager` storage save after command execution is omitted. Destruction markers indicate when the temporary parser and command are no longer referenced in this interaction, rather than when Java garbage collection occurs. The `CommandResult` remains alive because it is returned to the caller.

The undelete mechanism is facilitated by `ModelManager`, which keeps a stack, `deletedPersons`, of the persons deleted during the current session. Each entry is a `DeletedPerson` record holding the deleted `Person` and the index in the address book that they were deleted from. `ModelManager` exposes the stack through three `Model` operations:
* `Model#hasDeletedPersons()` — Returns true if there is a deleted person that can be restored.
* `Model#getLastDeletedPerson()` — Returns the most recently deleted person, without restoring them.
* `Model#restoreLastDeletedPerson()` — Reinserts the most recently deleted person at their original index, removes them from the stack, and resets the filtered person list to show all persons.

`Model#deletePerson()` pushes an entry onto the stack after it removes the person, so every successful `delete` can be reversed. `clear` replaces the address book through `Model#setAddressBook()` instead, so it does not add to the stack.
Given below is an example usage scenario and how the undelete mechanism behaves at each step.
Step 1. The user launches the application. `deletedPersons` is empty, so `undelete` fails with an error.
Step 2. The user executes `delete 1a2b3c4` to delete Benson, the 2nd person in the address book. `Model#deletePerson()` pushes `(Benson, 1)` onto `deletedPersons`.
Step 3. The user executes `delete 0f9e8d7` to delete Alice, the 1st person. `Model#deletePerson()` pushes `(Alice, 0)`, which is now on top of `(Benson, 1)`.

Step 4. The user realises that deleting Alice was a mistake, and executes `undelete`. `UndeleteCommand` checks that there is a deleted person to restore, and that no person with the same identity as Alice already exists. It then calls `Model#restoreLastDeletedPerson()`, which reinserts Alice at index 0 and pops `(Alice, 0)` off the stack.
The following sequence diagram shows how the `undelete` command in step 4 goes through the `Logic` and `Model` components:

Step 5. The user executes `undelete` again. Benson is reinserted at index 1, so the address book is back in its original order, and `deletedPersons` is empty again.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If a person with the same name has been added since the delete (e.g. the user re-added Alice by hand), `UndeleteCommand` fails before calling `Model#restoreLastDeletedPerson()`, as restoring the deleted person would leave two persons with the same name. The entry stays on the stack, and the error message tells the user to rename the clashing person with `edit` and run `undelete` again.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If persons were removed after the delete without going through `Model#deletePerson()` (e.g. by `clear`), the original index can be past the end of the list. `Model#restoreLastDeletedPerson()` then appends the person to the end instead.
`deletedPersons` exists only in memory. It is not saved by `Storage`, and it is not part of `ModelManager#equals()`, so it is lost when the app closes.
**Aspect: What is stored to restore a deleted person:**
* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** Store only the deleted person and their index.
* Pros: Uses little memory, and does not affect any other command.
* **Alternative 2:** Save a copy of the whole address book before every change, and restore the copy.

* Cons: Uses memory in proportion to the address book size for every command. Restoring a copy also reverses every command made after it, e.g. reversing a delete would also remove a person added afterwards.
* Pros: The name states exactly what it reverses, so users do not expect it to reverse `add` or `edit`.
* Cons: Users who know `undo` from other applications may try that first.
* Cons: Users would expect it to reverse every command, not just `delete`.
**Aspect: Where the restored person is placed:**
* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** At the index they were deleted from.
* Pros: The list looks exactly as it did before the delete.
* Cons: The index must be stored, and clamped when the list has since become shorter.
* **Alternative 2:** At the end of the list, like `add`.
* Cons: The list order changes, and in a long list the restored person is harder to find.

* **CLI (Command Line Interface)**: A way of using an application by typing text commands, as in ClientConnect's command box
* **GUI (Graphical User Interface)**: A way of using an application through visual elements such as windows, lists, and cards
* **Hexadecimal**: Using the digits `0`–`9` and the letters `a`–`f`. UUIDs are written in hexadecimal
* **Insurance Agent**: Point of contact for insurance products, manages a list of insurance clients' information
* **Insurance Client**: Consumer of insurance products, with an associated insurance agent who has the client's contact information
* **Mainstream OS**: Windows, Linux, Unix, or macOS
* **MSS (Main Success Scenario)**: The steps of a use case in which everything goes as expected. Extensions describe what happens otherwise
* **Remark**: An optional free-text note stored with a client, e.g. `Likes to swim.`
* **Short UUID**: The first 7 hexadecimal characters of a client's UUID, shown as `#xxxxxxx` on the client's card
* **Tag**: An alphanumeric label attached to a client, e.g. `friends`. A client can have any number of tags

* **UUID (Universally Unique Identifier)**: A 32-character hexadecimal identifier given to each client when they are added, e.g. `1a2b3c4d-1000-0000-0000-000000000000`. It does not change when the client is edited
* **UUID prefix**: The first 7 to 32 hexadecimal characters of a UUID, ignoring dashes. Commands such as `delete`, `edit`, and `remark` use it to select a client

ClientConnect is a **desktop application for insurance agents to manage their client contacts, optimized for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI)** while retaining the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI).

It is built for agents who handle large client portfolios and many active leads. You can record clients, tag them (for example by policy type), add remarks, and find them again by name or tag, all by typing short commands. If you type quickly, ClientConnect lets you manage your clients faster than clicking through forms or scrolling a spreadsheet.
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Copy the file to the folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for ClientConnect.
1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar ClientConnect.jar`.
A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. Note how the app contains some sample data.
:bulb: Double-clicking the JAR file may not start the app on some systems, so use the `java -jar` command above.

Do not put the JAR file in a write-protected folder, such as a system folder or a read-only drive. The app saves its data and settings next to the JAR file and will not work properly if it cannot write there.
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com a/John street, block 123, #01-01` : Adds a contact named `John Doe`.
* `delete 1a2b3c4` : Deletes the contact whose card shows the short UUID `#1a2b3c4`.
* `remark 1a2b3c4 r/Likes to swim.` : Adds a remark to the contact whose card shows `#1a2b3c4`.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.
* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `n/NAME [t/TAG]` can be used as `n/John Doe t/friend` or as `n/John Doe`.
* Items followed by `…`​ can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[t/TAG]…​` may be omitted, or written as `t/friend` or `t/friend t/family`.
* Parameters with a prefix (such as `n/` or `p/`) can be in any order.
For example, if the command specifies `n/NAME p/PHONE_NUMBER`, `p/PHONE_NUMBER n/NAME` is also acceptable.
Parameters without a prefix must come first: the `SHORT_UUID` for `edit`, `remark` and `delete`, and the name keywords for `find`.
For example, `remark 1a2b3c4 r/Likes to swim.` works, but `remark r/Likes to swim. 1a2b3c4` does not.
* Extraneous parameters for commands that take no parameters, such as `help`, `list`, `exit`, and `clear`, are ignored.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.
### Identifying a person by short UUID
Commands that act on one existing person (`edit`, `remark` and `delete`) identify the person by their **short UUID**: the 7-character code shown as `#xxxxxxx` beside the name on each person's card.
* Type the code without the `#`. For example, for a card showing `#1a2b3c4`, type `delete 1a2b3c4`.
* The code is made of hexadecimal characters (`0`–`9` and `a`–`f`) and is case-insensitive.
* The code is matched against **every** person in the address book, not just the currently displayed list, so filtering with `find` does not affect which person is chosen.

* If two persons share a short UUID, the command fails instead of guessing. Type more characters of the person's full UUID, up to all 32, to pick one. `delete` and `remark` list the full UUID of each match; you can also find it in the data file. Dashes are ignored, so you can paste a full UUID.

When adding a person or editing a person's name, ClientConnect compares the new name with existing names and may display a non-blocking warning when it finds a likely typo. For example, entering `Jon Smith` when `John Smith` already exists produces a warning naming `John Smith` as a possible match. The warning is shown after the usual success message:
Warning: "Jon Smith" is very similar to existing entry "John Smith".
* ignores leading and trailing spaces, repeated internal spaces, and letter case;
* requires at least three characters and uses a stricter similarity requirement for short names;
* checks only the person's name, not phone numbers, email addresses, addresses, remarks, or tags; and
* does not warn for a case-only match, an exact duplicate, or the person currently being edited.
Additional or misplaced spaces are flagged separately. For example, `John  Smith` may warn about the existing `John Smith`.

The warning is advisory only. The add or edit command is still completed and the input is saved; ClientConnect does not ask for confirmation. If the warning identifies the intended existing person, review the result and correct it with another command if necessary. If the new entry is intentional, no further action is required.

* Updates the remark of the person with the given `SHORT_UUID`. See [Identifying a person by short UUID](#identifying-a-person-by-short-uuid).
* The `r/` prefix is compulsory. Omitting it results in an invalid command.
* To remove an existing remark, enter `r/` without any text after it.
* `remark 1a2b3c4 r/Likes to swim.` adds a remark to the contact whose card shows `#1a2b3c4`.
* `remark 1a2b3c4 r/` removes the remark from the contact whose card shows `#1a2b3c4`.
### Locating persons by name or tag: `find`
Finds persons whose names contain any given name keyword or whose tags match any given tag.
Supply at least one name keyword or tag. Put name keywords before any `t/` prefixes.

Anything typed after a `t/` is read as part of that tag, so `find t/friends Alice` looks for the tag `friends Alice` and fails with `Tag names should be alphanumeric`. Type `find Alice t/friends` instead.
* The search is case-insensitive; for example, `irfan` matches `Irfan`.
* Keyword order does not matter; for example, `Ibrahim Irfan` matches `Irfan Ibrahim`.
* Keywords without a prefix search only names. Each `t/TAG` searches only tags.
* Name keywords match any part of a name; for example, `Irf` matches `Irfan Ibrahim`.
* Tags are case-insensitive and must match completely; `t/friends` matches `Friends` but not `bestfriends`.
Use one `t/` prefix per tag. Empty tags and tags containing spaces or punctuation are invalid.
* Persons matching at least one name keyword or tag are returned (an `OR` search), and each person appears once.
This helps when you misremember part of a name, as only one keyword needs to match.
* `find Irfan` and `find irfan` return the same results because search is case-insensitive.
With the sample data, both return only `Irfan Ibrahim`.
After adding a person named `Irfan Mohammed`, both return `Irfan Ibrahim` and `Irfan Mohammed`, as shown below.
![Results for 'find irfan' after adding Irfan Mohammed](images/findIrfanResult.png)
* `find Irfan Roy` returns `Irfan Ibrahim` and `Roy Balakrishnan` from the sample data, because either `Irfan` or `Roy` matches.
* `find t/friends t/colleagues` returns persons tagged either `friends` or `colleagues`.
* `find Irfan t/friends` returns persons whose names contain `Irfan` or who have the `friends` tag.
Deletes the specified person from the address book.
* Deletes the person with the given `SHORT_UUID`. See [Identifying a person by short UUID](#identifying-a-person-by-short-uuid).
* `delete 1a2b3c4` deletes the person whose card shows `#1a2b3c4`.
* `delete 1a2b3c4d1` deletes the person whose UUID starts with `1a2b3c4d1`, when two persons share the short UUID `#1a2b3c4`.
* If no person has that UUID prefix, the command fails with `No person with UUID: 1a2b3c4`.
* If more than one person matches, the command fails and lists the full UUID and name of each match. Enter enough characters of the UUID to tell them apart.
Two persons sharing a short UUID is very rare, so `delete` with the short UUID from the card is almost always enough.
Clears all entries from the address book.
Restores the most recently deleted person, in case you deleted the wrong one.
* The person is restored with the same short UUID, at the position in the list they were deleted from. If a sort is active, the person appears wherever the sort order places them.
* Running `undelete` again restores the person deleted before that, and so on, back to the first delete since the app was opened.
* After a restore, the list shows all persons, so the restored person is always visible.
* `undelete` only reverses `delete`. It does not reverse `clear`, `add`, `edit` or other commands.
* Deleted persons can only be restored until the app is closed.
* `undelete` takes no parameters. Anything typed after it is treated as an invalid command format.
* `delete 1a2b3c4` followed by `undelete` restores the person whose card showed `#1a2b3c4`.
* If there is no deleted person to restore, the command fails with `No deleted persons to restore.`

* If a person with the same name has been added since the delete, the command fails with `Cannot undelete NAME: a person with the same name already exists.` and nothing is restored, because two persons cannot share a name (ignoring case). Rename that person with `edit`, then run `undelete` again.
ClientConnect automatically saves data after every command. You do not need to save manually.
ClientConnect data is saved automatically as a JSON file `[JAR file location]/data/addressbook.json`. Advanced users are welcome to update data directly by editing that data file.

If your changes make the data file invalid, ClientConnect starts with an empty address book at the next run. The invalid file remains on disk until you run a command (ClientConnect saves after every command). Still, we recommend backing up the file before editing it.

Furthermore, certain edits can cause ClientConnect to behave in unexpected ways (e.g., if a value entered is outside of the acceptable range). Therefore, edit the data file only if you are confident that you can update it correctly.
**Q**: How do I transfer my data to another computer?
**A**: Install the app on the other computer and overwrite the data file it creates with the data file from your previous ClientConnect home folder.
**CLI** (Command Line Interface) | A way of using an app by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
**GUI** (Graphical User Interface) | The windows, buttons and lists you see and click on.
**Home folder** | The folder containing the JAR file. The app stores its data and settings there.
**Hexadecimal** | The characters `0`–`9` and `a`–`f`. UUIDs are made only of these characters.
**JSON** | The text file format used to store your data in `data/addressbook.json`.

**Prefix** | The short label before a value in a command, such as `n/` for name or `t/` for tag. It tells the app which field the value belongs to.
**Short UUID** | The first 7 characters of a person's UUID, shown as `#xxxxxxx` on the person's card. `edit`, `remark` and `delete` use it to pick a person.
**Tag** | A one-word label attached to a person, such as `TermLife`, used to group and find persons.
**UUID** | A long, unique ID given to every person automatically when they are added. It does not change when you edit the person.
